overview: Jōmon is the modern name for related archaeological traditions across the Japanese archipelago, not one kingdom, ethnicity or government. During this card’s 4000 to 1500 BCE window, communities occupied forests, coasts, valleys and islands. People built pit houses, managed plants, hunted, fished, cooked in pottery, worked stone, bone, wood and lacquer, exchanged valued materials, and made graves and ritual places. Some settlements grew large; others were small or seasonal. The evidence changes by region and century, so a single smooth border cannot contain the whole story. Archaeologists currently place the much longer Jōmon period roughly from 13,000 BCE to 400 BCE. The atlas begins late and stops midway, then redraws the same broad tradition under “Late Jomon Culture.” It also labels much of eastern and northern Jōmon Japan “Ainu” thousands of years before historically recognizable Ainu culture formed. This card keeps the atlas dates visible while refusing those shortcuts. There are no known contemporary Jōmon texts. Potsherds, food residues, houses, burials, teeth, DNA, pollen and even ancient poop must do the talking.

periods.title: Later Early Jōmon communities in varied landscapes
periods.summary: Official broad chronologies place 4000 BCE within Early Jōmon, but boundaries differ by region and calibration. Villages, pottery and intensive coastal and woodland use were already well established without one archipelago-wide political center.

periods.title: Regional concentration and the opening of Middle Jōmon
periods.summary: In some eastern and northern districts, settlements became larger and craft styles more elaborate. Sannai-Maruyama began around 3900 BCE, yet house counts accumulated across centuries and cannot be read as one census.

periods.title: Middle Jōmon settlement and exchange networks
periods.summary: Many regional sequences place these centuries within Middle Jōmon. Pottery styles, managed plant resources and exchange in obsidian, jade and other materials linked communities without evidence for a unified state or capital.

periods.title: Late Middle Jōmon change, not a single collapse
periods.summary: Large settlements and networks changed at different tempos. Radiocarbon summaries show regional peaks and declines rather than one nationwide disaster, while communities reorganized houses, subsistence and gathering places.

periods.title: A regionally uneven Middle-to-Late transition
periods.summary: Archaeological phase boundaries are tools for sorting pottery and sites, not dates when everyone changed identity. Some large settlements contracted while local fishing, hunting, plant use and craft traditions continued in new combinations.

periods.title: First half of Late Jōmon in the indexed interval
periods.summary: The Oyu circles date to approximately 2000 to 1500 BCE and show coordinated gathering, burial and stone movement. The atlas endpoint closes this card, but neither Jōmon lifeways nor the archaeological period ended there.

sections.title: Read the map, the dates and the silence

items.text: The live index calls this record “Jōmon,” classifies it as a culture and gives approximate dates of 4000 to 1500 BCE. Its ledger has three observed intervals and began with an imported summary but no More info card or review. Archaeologists use Jōmon for a far longer, internally varied period, not a state.

At 4000, 3000 and 2000 BCE the target is a three-part MultiPolygon with three rings and 180 positions. Its coordinate hashes are c54979e7023b2f070927c6a319a852529c6acb21bf9f6cbb363a31598ce728a9, ca9717e966f9bd5eeaab41e0cf4b85ee4d5fad1f5a51bd080befb49f46a51b58 and 62259c5e827b79c28439706353ec24c07b302b1f69ad5254d0de344131eebe92. Tiny coordinate drift does not turn these display shapes into ancient borders. The outline remains a modern visualization convention.

The polygon includes test points near Kanazawa, Nagoya, Torihama, Osaka, Kochi, Fukuoka, Nagasaki and Uenohara. It excludes Sannai-Maruyama, Goshono, Oyu, Korekawa, Sendai, Tokyo, Kasori and all tested Hokkaido points, even though many are major Jōmon sites. The shape is therefore an atlas partition, not the culture’s real extent.

At 1500 BCE the exact target vanishes and a broader layer named “late-jomon-culture” appears across much of Honshu, Shikoku and Kyushu. At 400 BCE the atlas divides a western Yayoi layer from an eastern Late Jōmon layer. These are cartographic seams, not synchronized migrations, conquests or identity changes.

Contemporaneous written-language sample: none is securely known. 縄文, read Jōmon and often translated “cord pattern,” is a modern Japanese archaeological label, not something Jōmon people wrote or called themselves. With no surviving texts, researchers read pottery sequences, residues, houses, pollen, tools, skeletons, DNA, burials and sediments instead.

sections.title: Live with forests, coasts and changing settlements

items.text: There was no standard Jōmon landscape. Officially nominated northern sites range from bays, rivers and terraces to mountain foothills. Elsewhere, island and inland ecologies offered different fish, shellfish, nuts, game and timber. Seasonal abundance helped some communities stay in one place, but mobility and settlement size varied greatly.

A pit-house stain is not a frozen family photograph. Houses were rebuilt, abandoned and overlapped across centuries, so the number excavated at a site is usually much larger than the number standing together. Researchers combine radiocarbon dates, pottery sequences and spatial relationships before estimating village size or permanence.

Sannai-Maruyama, occupied about 3900 to 2200 BCE, preserves ordinary pit houses, storage pits, long buildings and six-post structures. A reconstructed pit house may look cozy, but smoke, damp and maintenance were daily realities. Its spectacular scale illuminates one regional hub, not a capital governing the archipelago.

At coastal Kitakogane, shell deposits, animal bones and tools record a settlement tied to marine foods. A spring area held deliberately broken grinding stones, while burials occupied another part of the site. Water, food processing, refuse and ceremony met in a carefully used landscape, rather than separate modern-looking zones.

Some communities arranged houses, storage pits, graves and dumping places in repeated patterns; others left much lighter traces. More than 500 pit-house remains at Sannai accumulated over a long occupation. Archaeologists can map organized cooperation, but that does not reveal a mayor, king, tax office or permanent ruling class.

sections.title: Find, grow, cook and share food

items.text: Jōmon meals mixed many resources: fish and shellfish near water, deer and wild boar in forests, plus nuts, roots and other plants. At Torihama, pottery lipids strongly emphasize aquatic foods while grinding stones and plant remains reveal foods those lipids miss. One laboratory method never recovers the whole menu.

Cooking pots changed what people could eat by making broth, rendering fats and softening ingredients. Chemical residues in much earlier vessels identify fish and other aquatic products, proving that pottery mattered before farming. For this later card period, the result is a useful warning: “hunter-gatherer” never meant “no cuisine.”

Chestnut trees and lacquer trees could be encouraged near settlements, making useful groves part of a managed environment. Management demanded planning, pruning, harvesting and knowledge passed over years. It sits between a cartoon of untouched wilderness and a cartoon of plowed fields, and it differed by region.

Seed-size changes in soybean, adzuki bean and barnyard grass have been used to argue for cultivation or domestication. The debate is lively because bigger seeds alone do not reconstruct a farm. Direct plant remains, dating and local context matter, so the safest picture includes experiments and tending without declaring universal agriculture.

Kitakogane’s shells and fish bones suggest heavy marine use, while dental evidence there includes remarkably few cavities. That combination belongs to one community and time, not every Jōmon mouth. A child elsewhere might eat nut porridge, smoked fish or roasted roots, but no surviving recipe says what was for Tuesday dinner.

sections.title: Make pottery, lacquer, stone and bone work

items.text: Pottery was technology, container and visual language. Cord impressions are only one family of surface treatment; forms and decoration shifted dramatically between regions and phases. Clay recipes, firing and repairs reveal choices. Carbon dates, microscopic inclusions and residues let archaeologists test those choices rather than judging a pot only by its dramatic handles.

Residue science reads molecules absorbed into pottery walls, including lipids that survive after a meal has vanished. It can distinguish broad resource groups, but it does not print an ingredient list. Plants may leave weak signals, reuse mixes meals and soil can contaminate samples, so laboratory evidence works best beside bones and seeds.

Lacquer craft was astonishingly technical. Makers tapped sap that can irritate skin, prepared surfaces, added pigments or fillers and built controlled layers that improved durability, adhesion and water resistance. Archaeological cross-sections show recipes rather than one accidental smear. A shiny comb or bowl represents patient chemistry learned without a textbook.

Waterlogged sites preserve things that ordinary dry soil eats for breakfast: baskets, cordage, textiles, wooden bows, bark objects and dugout canoes. Such finds expose a huge “missing” craft economy. Clothing probably used plant fibers and hides, but complete outfits are rare enough that confident Jōmon fashion catalogs belong in the imagination aisle.

Stone axes cut wood, points tipped arrows, grinding stones processed plants, and bone or antler became hooks, needles and harpoon parts. Tool wear and manufacturing debris can reveal tasks and repair. They cannot automatically reveal the worker’s age or gender, so labels like “men hunted, women sewed” require evidence, not habit.

sections.title: Connect communities without inventing an empire

items.text: Geochemical fingerprints trace some obsidian in Middle Jōmon Kanto to Kozushima, an island source reached across open water. Network analysis shows connections changing through time. The stone may have moved hand to hand, by visiting specialists or through voyages; its arrival proves contact, not a named trade company or treaty.

Jade artifacts can be mineralogically linked to the Itoigawa area on the Japan Sea coast. Ornaments carried color, labor and perhaps social meaning far from the source. Their distribution maps routes of movement and preference, but an exotic bead does not by itself identify its owner’s rank or the language of a trader.

Sannai-Maruyama yielded jade, amber, obsidian and asphalt whose sources lay far beyond the settlement; some materials traveled hundreds of kilometers. Local workshops transformed part of that flow. This was impressive connectivity among communities, yet no coins, written prices or central customs office survive to show a single regulated market.

Dugout canoes demonstrate the equipment needed for coasts, rivers and straits, though one preserved hull cannot tell us its exact cargo. Seaborne material routes and island obsidian make voyaging visible. Weather, currents and repair skills would have shaped every trip, and many paddles left no heroic travel diary.

Archaeologists often call Jōmon communities “complex hunter-gatherers” because some were settled, stored food, exchanged rare goods and built substantial places. The phrase describes patterns, not a halfway point on a ladder toward states. Regional histories could grow, contract or reorganize without marching toward kings, armies and bureaucracy.

At Sannai-Maruyama, adults were buried in pits beside paths, while some infants or children were placed in reused pottery containers with holes. Location and treatment show that age mattered in mortuary practice. They do not tell us one universal belief about an afterlife, because no accompanying explanation was written down.

Oyu’s two great stone circles used river stones arranged around central features, with graves, pits and buildings nearby. Their axes relate to the summer-solstice sunset, suggesting attention to sky and season. “Calendar” is a tempting shortcut; the remains securely show repeated planning, gathering and burial, not an instruction manual for astronomy.

Clay figurines, stone settings, deposits and carefully broken objects indicate repeated ritual acts, yet their meanings remain debated. The World Heritage evaluation emphasizes a long development of ritual places. Calling every figurine a goddess, toy or doctor would replace evidence with a modern story, so the card keeps several possibilities open.

Some dogs received deliberate burials, and later patterns have been linked to their value in forest hunting, where a dog could track or hold wounded game. Tender placement is real evidence of special treatment. “Beloved pet exactly like mine” is possible but unprovable, which dogs would probably find unnecessarily fussy.

A closely placed adult woman and child in one Jōmon double burial looked like a family pair, but ancient DNA found they were not maternally related. They still may have shared another social bond. The result is a wonderful warning that grave closeness, house proximity and modern family expectations are not genetic proof.

sections.title: Grow up, learn and organize social life

items.text: Houses probably sheltered cooking, sleeping, repair and storytelling, but archaeologists cannot simply count one nuclear family per floor. Buildings changed use and household membership may have extended beyond biological kin. Even a shared burial need not mean parent and child, so “family” must include social care as well as DNA.

Clay tablets preserve the pressed feet of babies or small children. Some came from burial contexts, and museums interpret them as connected with remembrance or prayer. The toe marks are direct and delightfully human; the exact ceremony is not. A tiny footprint is evidence of a child, not a complete biography.

Late Jōmon house-floor areas in southern Kanto produce relatively low measured inequality in a large modern study. That does not prove perfect equality: house size is only one wealth proxy, and prestige, skill, food access or ritual authority may hide elsewhere. It does challenge the reflex to invent palaces wherever craft is beautiful.

No schoolrooms, alphabets or lesson books survive. Children could learn by watching and joining food gathering, clay preparation, cord making, tool repair and seasonal journeys. Skilled products imply teaching and practice, but archaeology rarely identifies the teacher. The safest classroom reconstruction is a task shared beside experienced hands.

Children surely played, but play is one of archaeology’s escape artists. Footprints capture children’s bodies, while figurines and small clay objects do not automatically become toys. Tag, teasing and make-believe leave almost nothing behind, so a funny-looking object is not permission to announce the world’s oldest action figure.

sections.title: Spend a day at home and at work

items.text: A pit dwelling was dug below ground level, framed with wood and covered with organic roofing, usually around a hearth. At Sannai-Maruyama many ordinary examples were roughly three to four meters across, while a few buildings were much larger. Size and function varied, and reconstructions necessarily supply vanished roofs and walls.

Clothing is much harder to recover than pottery. Rare waterlogged fibers, baskets and cordage show spinning, twisting, plaiting and weaving skills; hides could vanish altogether. Ornaments survive more often than shirts. Anyone offering a single “authentic Jōmon outfit” for four millennia and a whole archipelago is overselling the wardrobe.

Daily work changed with season and place: collect nuts, fish a run, tend useful trees, hunt, cut fuel, patch a roof, shape a hook, grind food and mend containers. Toolkits reveal tasks but seldom who performed them. Age, ability, experience and local custom likely divided labor more flexibly than modern cartoons.

A meal might be boiled, roasted, dried or smoked, and pots could be reused for different ingredients. Residues preserve fats better than flavor, so salt, leafy plants and seasonings may disappear from the chemical story. The evidence can reveal aquatic cooking traditions, but it cannot certify “Jōmon stew” on a modern café menu.

Dogs worked near humans as hunting partners in at least some regions, and their burials show that certain animals received careful treatment. They also ate, barked, got injured and required attention. Calling every dog a pet is too simple, but treating them as equipment with fur misses the social evidence.

Teeth record both meals and misery. A study across thirteen sites found cavity rates changed by region and through time, with increases in some Middle and later groups. Starchy or sticky plant foods can feed tooth decay. There was no single “Jōmon diet,” and one beautiful skull cannot stand for everyone.

Skeletal remains also show periodontal disease, tooth loss, heavy muscle use and occasional serious injuries. Bone records conditions that leave marks and people who survived long enough to remodel tissue; it misses most fevers, stomach illnesses and short episodes. Health estimates therefore have a built-in survivor and preservation bias.

No Jōmon medical manual identifies a healer, diagnosis or remedy. Healed injuries prove survival and may suggest care, but not the treatment used. Plants certainly surrounded people and some could have soothed or harmed; without residues in a secure therapeutic context, naming a pharmacy would be guesswork rather than history.

Springs, streams and wells of naturally collected water mattered for drinking, cooking and craft. At Kitakogane a spring became a special deposition place; at later Korekawa, water helped leach bitterness from horse chestnuts. These are site-specific practices, not evidence for pipes, municipal sewers or a universal water system.

No securely identified standard Jōmon toilet structure is known. Preserved human coprolites in shell middens may mean people sometimes used refuse deposits, but the precise arrangement is still under investigation. Ancient poop reveals food and parasites; it does not reveal whether anyone complained about whose turn it was to cover the midden.

sections.title: Change without a fake fall or simple replacement

items.text: A large skeletal survey found violent deaths rare and highly restricted in Jōmon samples. That argues against routine archipelago-wide warfare, not against every assault or dispute. No evidence here supports state armies, prisons, taxes or forced labor. Coercion may have existed within relationships, but its institutions are not securely recoverable.

Settlement counts and radiocarbon dates rise and fall differently by region, especially around Middle and Late Jōmon. Climate, resources, mobility and counting methods all complicate the curves. A village shrinking could reflect relocation or changing house use, so “collapse” should never be pasted across the entire archipelago without local proof.

The atlas stops this id at 1500 BCE, then immediately draws “Late Jomon Culture.” Archaeological chronologies continue Late and Final Jōmon for many centuries. Nothing in the map data demonstrates extinction, conquest or a fall in 1500 BCE; this is a renamed coverage layer, so the card records continuity and leaves successors empty.

Wet-rice farming appeared first in northern Kyushu centuries later and spread east unevenly. Migrants, local foragers, new crops and older cooking habits interacted over long transitions. Yayoi is another archaeological category, not a single army that replaced everybody overnight, and the starting date differs substantially between regions.

Historically recognizable Ainu culture formed much later through Epi-Jōmon, Satsumon, Okhotsk and other northern histories. Ryukyuan islands followed several distinct trajectories, with Jōmon-related ancestry plus later mixture. Genetics can trace relationships, not freeze culture. The atlas’s 4000 BCE “Ainu” layer is anachronistic, and neither Ainu nor Ryukyuans are living fossils.

ending.text: The atlas’s Jōmon id ends at approximately 1500 BCE, but Jōmon archaeological traditions continued for many centuries and changed at different speeds across the archipelago. The next atlas layer is simply labeled “Late Jomon Culture.” Much later, wet-rice farming, migration and mixture contributed to regionally timed Yayoi transitions, while northern and island histories took other paths. Communities, skills and ancestry continued through those changes. This endpoint is therefore continuity in a relabeled map layer, not a fall, conquest or extinction.
